stimulus.text: When independence was won, Americans agreed the new government would be a republic — a country in which sovereignty, or power, ultimately rested with the people rather than a monarch. This was a radical move: there had been virtually no republics in the world since the Roman republic two thousand years earlier. For many Americans, republicanism also implied a moral stance. Republican citizens were independent people who embodied civic virtue, putting the interests of the community above their own self-interest, and leading industrious, simple lives.

books.section: B. Common Sense, the Declaration of Independence, and Republican Self-Government

stem: What made choosing a republic a radical move in 1776?

options.text: Sovereignty would rest with the people, not a monarch, with almost no republics since Rome
Republics had been the most common form of government across Europe for centuries
options.misconception: The passage says the opposite — there had been virtually no republics since the Roman republic.

options.text: A republic would give the king more power than he had held under Parliament
options.misconception: A republic has no king at all. Sovereignty rests with the people, not with a strengthened monarch.

options.text: Republics required every adult citizen to serve in the army for life
options.misconception: The passage says nothing about lifelong army service — it describes civic virtue, not conscription.

rationales.A: Putting sovereignty with the people instead of a monarch broke with two thousand years of monarchy — that is what made it radical. The newness is the point: power had almost never sat with the people.
rationales.B: Republics were rare, not common. The passage stresses there had been virtually none since Rome.
rationales.C: A republic removes the king, it does not strengthen him. Power moves to the people.
rationales.D: Lifelong army service is not in the passage. Republican virtue meant community over self-interest, not conscription.
rationales.general:
1. Find where sovereignty sits. In a republic it rests with the people, not a monarch.
2. Ask how new that was. Virtually no republics had existed since Rome, two thousand years earlier.
3. Put the two together. Handing power to the people after centuries of kings is the radical move.
Remember: to judge how radical a change is, measure it against what came before — here, two thousand years of monarchy.
